name: Steps
tagline: A comparator and a stepper in one. Walks a voltage up and down inside a window you set.

sections.panelMap:
STEPS pairs a window comparator with a stepper. The stepper adds a fixed STEP to its output every time it's triggered, and the comparator watches whether that voltage has left the window set by BIAS and RANGE. Use it to build fixed-interval scales of any width, count steps, or make rhythms out of the window crossings.

The top half is the comparator. The bottom half is the stepper. With nothing patched into the comparator IN, the two halves are wired together: the stepper's output feeds the comparator, and the comparator's gates push the stepper back into the window when it walks out.

[[fig:normals]]

Comparator:
- IN: the signal to compare. Patching it breaks the normal to the stepper, so the two halves work independently.
- BIAS knob: center of the window, ±5V.
- RANGE knob: size of the window, 0–10V.
- OUT + / OUT −: 10V gates that go high when IN is above or below the window.
- IN, BIAS and RANGE each have a CV jack with an attenuator knob above it.

Stepper:
- STEP: step size, ±1V. Each mark on the knob is 2 semitones. The IN jack below adds to the knob through its attenuator, scaled so ±5V sweeps the whole knob range.
- TRIG.: takes one step. The button above it does the same.
- RESET: jumps back to BIAS (or to 0V when the comparator normal is broken). Also has a button.
- INVERT STEP: a gate here flips the sign of STEP + IN, so the stepper walks the other way.
- OUT (bottom right): the stepper voltage.

Lights: the column shows where the stepper sits in the window, in 10% steps. The larger light flashes on each step or reset.

How the normal works: when the stepper walks out of the window, the comparator gates add ±RANGE back into the next step. The correction lands one step late, which is where a lot of the module's variation comes from.

Context menu:
- Poly Channel Count: Auto follows the widest input, or lock it to 1–16 channels.
- Quantization: snaps the stepper OUT to a grid. Octaves, 12-EDO semitones, 24-EDO quarter-tones, or 9, 17, 19, 22, 31, 41 and 53-EDO.
- Invert Input Mode: Momentary (default) inverts while the INVERT STEP gate is high. Latch flips direction on each gate.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the window:
   - BIAS places the center, RANGE sets the width.

2. Set the step:
   - Turn STEP to the interval you want. At 1/12V per step you're walking semitones; turn on 12-EDO quantization to keep them exact.

3. Step it:
   - Patch a clock to TRIG. Patch a slower clock to RESET to start the walk over.

4. Read the outputs:
   - The bottom OUT is your stepped CV.
   - The OUT + and OUT − gates fire when the walk crosses the window, which makes them handy clock dividers.

5. Split it in two:
   - Patch something into the comparator IN to use the comparator and stepper as two separate tools.
sections.patching:
• Counting: The ratio of RANGE to STEP sets how many steps fit in the window. With RANGE at 4V and STEP at 1V, a comparator gate fires once every four steps.

• Shifting rhythms: Modulate STEP with an LFO and take the OUT + and OUT − gates as clock divisions. As the step size drifts, the divisions change.

• Melodic walks: Patch the stepper OUT to an oscillator's V/oct. Turn on quantization for in-tune intervals.

• Sequence the phrase, not the notes: Drive BIAS, RANGE and STEP from a slow sequencer. Each stage sets up a new walk, so you're sequencing contour and phrasing instead of single notes.

• Up and down: Patch OUT + into INVERT STEP with Invert Input Mode set to Latch. The stepper climbs to the top of the window and turns around.

figures.caption: With the comparator IN unpatched, the stepper and comparator are normalled together: STEP and IN feed the stepper, and the comparator outputs feed back into it.
The comparator +OUT gate as the stepper crosses the top of the window.
STEPPER OUT climbing by STEP on each trigger. When it leaves the window (BIAS ± RANGE), the normalled comparator knocks it back by RANGE one step later.

name: Envelope Array
tagline: Six related envelopes from one set of controls. Set the first and last, and the four in between fill in.

sections.panelMap:
ENVELOPE ARRAY generates six envelopes that belong together. You set the width of the first and last, and the four in between take evenly spaced widths. SLANT and CURVE shape all six at once. Each channel has its own trigger input and an end-of-cycle gate, so the module is easy to self-patch into LFOs, chains and loops.

Controls:
- FIRST WIDTH: cycle time of channel 1. CV can push it beyond the knob's range.
- LAST WIDTH: cycle time of channel 6. Channels 2–5 sit between FIRST and LAST.
- RANGE buttons: one each for FIRST and LAST. Choose fast, seconds or minutes. The in-between channels bridge the two even if they're set to different ranges.
- SLANT: tilts every envelope between a fast rise and a fast fall.
- CURVE: log to linear to exponential, and beyond to the extremes.
- BUTTON: triggers channel 1 by hand.
SLANT and CURVE also nudge the width a little.

[[fig:shapes]]

Jacks:
- TRIGGER/GATE INPUTS 1–6: trigger inputs. Each is normalled to the one on its right, so a single trigger into 1 fires all six.
- ENVELOPES 1–6: the envelope outputs.
- GATES 1–6: go high while their envelope is at 0V. Use them to chain, loop and reset.
- SLANT, CURVE, FIRST and LAST each have a CV input with an attenuverter.

Context menu:
- Enable Retriggering: by default a channel won't retrigger until it has fallen back to 0V. With this on, it retriggers anywhere in the fall (but still not during the rise).
- Enable Polyphonic Output to Channel 1: ENVELOPES 1 and GATES 1 carry all six channels as one poly cable.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the widths:
   - Pick a RANGE for each end, then set FIRST and LAST. The middle four fill in between.

2. Shape them:
   - SLANT and CURVE shape all six together. Try the corners of the two knobs first. The figure above shows what's possible.

3. Trigger:
   - One trigger into input 1 fires all six, because the inputs are normalled to the right. Patch separate triggers to break the chain.

4. Use the gates:
   - The GATE outputs mark the end of each envelope. Patch them into other inputs to chain, loop or reset things.

5. Modulate:
   - Every shape and width control has a CV input with an attenuverter.
sections.patching:
• Related modulation: Send the six envelopes to six filter cutoffs or VCAs. They move together but not in lockstep, which keeps a patch alive without sounding random.

• Six LFOs: Patch each channel's GATE back into its own input. Each envelope retriggers itself as it finishes, so you get six free-running LFOs that drift in and out of phase.

[[fig:six-lfos]]

• Chained envelopes: Patch GATE 1 into input 2, GATE 2 into input 3, and so on. Each envelope starts the next. Patch GATE 6 back into input 1 to loop the whole chain. Use the envelope outputs to modulate the module's own controls for patterns that keep changing.

[[fig:chain]]

• Rhythms: Patch the GATE outputs into sequencer resets, and let the envelope widths set the pattern.

• Sub-harmonics: Set both ranges to audio rate. Patch an oscillator into input 1 and set FIRST a little shorter than its wavelength (SIGNALS helps here). Mix all six envelopes and offset the mix by -5V (VCV RSCL works). Each channel can only retrigger at the end of its own cycle, so they lock to the oscillator in overlapping ways and produce rich sub-harmonics.

[[fig:subharmonics]]

figures.caption: SLANT and CURVE together cover a wide range of envelope shapes.
Six LFOs: each GATE patched back into its own input.
Chained envelopes: each GATE triggers the next channel, and GATE 6 loops back to input 1.
Sub-harmonics: an oscillator triggers the array at audio rate, and the six envelopes are mixed and offset.

name: Penta Sequencer
tagline: Five steps, five outputs at once. Each trigger rotates which knob goes to which output, with slew that follows your tempo.

sections.panelMap:
PENTA SEQUENCER plays all five of its steps at the same time. Each output A–E carries one of the knobs I–V, and every trigger rotates which knob goes where. Two paths decide the rotation, Circle and Star, and you can run either one clockwise or counterclockwise. SLEW is computed from your trigger timing, so glides stay in time when the tempo changes.

Controls:
- KNOBS I–V: the five step voltages, ±5V.
- SLEW: off at the left. Turned up, each output glides to its next value, timed from the last trigger interval and the size of the jump. CV into the center jack overrides the knob: -5V to +5V, with 0V giving 50% slew.

Inputs:
- TRIG: advances the rotation one step. The button does the same.
- RESET: back to the start (A plays I). Also has a button.
- CIRCLE / STAR: Circle by default (I→II→III→IV→V→I). Hold a gate above 1V for Star (I→III→V→II→IV→I).
- CW / CCW: clockwise by default. Hold a gate above 1V to run counterclockwise. Changing direction swaps the left and right outputs.
- SHIFT: transposes all five steps.

Outputs:
- The five round jacks around the pentagon are outputs A–E. The lights around each one show which knob it's playing, and a light by the knobs marks the one feeding the bottom-most active output.

Context menu:
- Enable Polyphonic Output to Channel A: output A carries all five outputs as one poly cable.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the steps:
   - Dial in five voltages on I–V.

2. Clock it:
   - Patch a clock into TRIG. Each trigger rotates the knob-to-output mapping, and all five outputs change at once.

3. Change the path:
   - A gate into CIRCLE / STAR switches to Star while it's held.
   - A gate into CW / CCW runs the rotation backwards while it's held.

4. Add slew:
   - Turn up SLEW to glide between steps. Bigger jumps glide faster, so the outputs always arrive by the next trigger.
sections.patching:
• Slewed octaves: Set the knobs to -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and SLEW to 0.25. Send each output to a wavetable VCO with a slightly different timbre. For melody, run a second PENTA SEQUENCER with slew at 0, quantize it, and patch it into the first one's SHIFT. The octave lanes glide while the notes stay in tune.

• Five LFOs: Clock slowly and set SLEW to 1.0. The slew uses the time between the last two triggers to build its ramps, so you get five slow, related LFOs.

[[fig:slew]]

• Fixed root: Reset so the bottom output plays the step you want as your root. Switch between Circle, Star, CW and CCW as much as you like; the bottom output stays put.

• Five-channel fader: Set knob I to +5V and the rest to 0V. Patch each output to a mixer channel's level and set SLEW to 1. Each slow trigger crossfades to the next channel. Good for moving between soundscapes.

[[fig:fader]]

figures.caption: SLEW morphs continuously from stepped to sloped CV. Knobs set to I=0V, II=1.25V, III=2.5V, IV=3.75V, V=5V.
Five-channel fader: one knob at 5V rotates across the outputs, and SLEW turns each step into a crossfade.

name: Impulse Controller
tagline: Fire an impulse into a 24-node network and watch it ripple out. Every node is an envelope output.

sections.panelMap:
IMPULSE CONTROLLER sends a pulse through a branching network of 24 nodes. Each node rings with its own decay envelope when the pulse reaches it, then wakes the nodes after it. You get 24 related envelopes that fire in rhythm with your input, spread out in time like a wave moving through a medium.

Controls (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- LAG: how long a pulse takes to travel from one node to the next.
- SPREAD: how the nodes line up in time. Turn left to pull them into unison, right to spread them apart.
- DECAY: how long each node rings once it's hit.

[[fig:network]]

Jacks:
- IN: a gate or trigger here fires the first node. The button above does the same.
- IMPULSES: 24 envelope outputs. The light next to each one shows its level, and the red trail shows the pulse moving through the network.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the shape of the wave:
   - LAG sets the travel time between nodes, DECAY sets how long each node rings.

2. Fire it:
   - Patch a clock or gate into IN, or press the button.

3. Adjust SPREAD:
   - A node can only pass the pulse on once it has decayed below a threshold, and SPREAD sets that threshold. At the far left, nodes fire in unison.
   - SPREAD also scales the timing down the network. Negative SPREAD makes each later node fire sooner; positive SPREAD stretches each step to 1–2x longer.

[[fig:threshold]]

[[fig:spread]]

4. Patch the outputs:
   - Treat the 24 outputs as a bank of related envelopes. Send them to VCAs, filters, panners or other modules' CV inputs.
sections.patching:
• Moving sound: Send groups of outputs to the pan or level CVs of a mixer. Each pulse sweeps across the stereo field as it travels through the network.

• Related modulation: Patch different nodes to different parameters. Everything moves together but never quite in sync.

• Self-patched networks: Patch node outputs back into IN, or into LAG, SPREAD and DECAY. Press the button to start it, then watch the pulse circulate. Patching several IMPULSE CONTROLLERs into each other builds bigger rhythmic networks.

figures.caption: How the 24 nodes connect. The pulse enters at node 1 and branches outward.
A node passes the pulse on once its envelope decays below the threshold set by SPREAD.
SPREAD also scales node timing, shortening or stretching the gap at each step down the network.

name: Signals
tagline: A six-channel scope that fits in your signal path. Good for tuning envelopes and LFOs.

sections.panelMap:
SIGNALS shows six signals at once in a narrow module, and passes each one straight through so you can leave it in the patch. It's handy for dialing in envelope and LFO shapes.

Controls:
- RANGE knob: time window, up to 1 second.
- SLOW switch: stretches the window to 10 seconds.
- RETRIG button: with the light on, each trace restarts on a rising edge through 1V, so envelopes stand still on the screen. Turn it off for free-running signals.

Jacks:
- Inputs (left): six signals. A polyphonic cable fills the channels below it until the next patched input.
- PASS outputs (right): each input passes through unchanged.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch up to six signals into the inputs.
2. Use the PASS outputs to carry on to wherever the signals were going.
3. Set the time window with RANGE. Flip SLOW for LFOs and long envelopes.
4. Leave RETRIG on to freeze repeating envelopes in place. Turn it off to watch signals roll past.
sections.patching:
• Envelope tuning: Put SIGNALS between an envelope and its VCA. With RETRIG on, the shape holds still while you turn the knobs.

• Compare a family: Patch all six outputs of ENVELOPE ARRAY or HEX MOD in at once to see how they relate.

• Setting up audio-rate tricks: Use a short RANGE to check wavelengths, for example when setting FIRST WIDTH for the ENVELOPE ARRAY sub-harmonics patch.

name: Ranges
tagline: Evenly spaced voltages between TOP and BOTTOM. Scales, crossfades, panning and gate scanning.

sections.panelMap:
RANGES fills in the voltages between TOP and BOTTOM in equal steps. DIVS sets how many steps, and one more output lights up for each. Because everything is under CV, the same module works as an interval generator, a multi-way crossfader, a panning spreader or a gate scanner.

Controls (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- TOP: voltage of the top output, ±10V. Adds to its CV.
- BOTTOM: voltage of the bottom active output, ±10V. Adds to its CV.
- DIVS: number of divisions, 0–12. Each volt of CV adds about 2.4 divisions.

Jacks:
- OUTS: up to 13 outputs, from TOP down to BOTTOM. The lights show which are active. Inactive outputs sit at 0V.
- TOP and BOTTOM are polyphonic: patch poly cables in and every output becomes a poly cable.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set TOP and BOTTOM.
2. Set DIVS. The outputs in between are evenly spaced.
3. Patch the outputs anywhere you need a set of related voltages.
sections.patching:
• Chromatic scale: TOP 0V, BOTTOM 1V, DIVS 12. Each output is one semitone higher than the last.

• Perfect fourths: TOP 0V, BOTTOM 5V, DIVS 12. Each step is 5/12V, a perfect fourth.

• Crossfader: Patch two signals into the TOP and BOTTOM inputs with both attenuverters at 1 and both knobs at 0. The outputs are blends of the two, from all TOP to all BOTTOM. Change DIVS for more or fewer blends.

• Group panning: Set TOP and BOTTOM to 0 with attenuverters at 1. Patch -5V and +5V into a crossfader (VCV FADE works) and its outputs into TOP and BOTTOM. Set DIVS to your number of mixer channels and patch the outputs to the pan CVs. Moving the fader pans every channel at once.

• Gate scanner: TOP 5V, BOTTOM 5V, DIVS 0. Patch outputs 3 and up to gate inputs. A rising voltage into DIVS turns them on one by one.

name: Hex Mod
tagline: Six phase-related LFOs. NODES rearranges their phases from evenly spread to unison and back.

sections.panelMap:
HEX MOD is six sine LFOs running at one rate. NODES sets how their phases are arranged around the cycle: evenly spread in a hexagon, all together, or grouped in twos and threes. A trigger on any channel pulls its phase back to zero, and it eases back into place afterwards.

Controls:
- RATE: speed of all six LFOs, up to 20 Hz. The button beside it switches to slow mode, where the knob covers 1/20 of the range. RATE has an attenuverter and CV input.
- NODES: phase arrangement. 0 = hexagonal (evenly spaced), 1 = unison, 2 = two groups, 3 = three groups. In between, it morphs. Attenuverter and CV.
- RANGE: output level, ±10V. The CV input lets RANGE act as a bipolar VCA.
- SYNC: locks the LFOs to an external clock or oscillator. By default, patching SYNC takes over from the RATE knob.

Jacks:
- PHASE RESET (top row): one per LFO. A trigger resets that output to zero phase. An envelope eases the phase back to its NODES position, and a gate holds the phase while it's high. Each input is normalled to the next, in a loop.
- Outputs: six LFOs, at the corners of the hexagon.

Lights: each output has 10 lights. Red lights are +1V each, blue lights are -1V each.

Context menu:
- Enable Lights: turns the lights off if you'd rather not have them blinking.
- Rate multiplies the Sync Input: RATE multiplies the synced clock instead of being ignored. RATE 1 follows the clock, RATE 2 doubles it.
- Sync locks both Clock and Phase: on by default, so each clock pulse also realigns the phases. Turn it off to let the phases run free and reset them with the PHASE RESET inputs.
- Rate input take v/oct (for audio rate): RATE CV tracks V/oct for audio-rate use. The RATE knob and attenuverter are disabled.
- Enable Polyphonic Output to Channel 1: output 1 carries all six LFOs.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the speed with RATE, and the phase arrangement with NODES.
2. Patch the six outputs to six destinations.
3. Patch triggers or envelopes into the PHASE RESET inputs to pull channels into line and let them drift back. One trigger into the first input resets all six, because they're normalled.
4. Patch a clock into SYNC to lock to tempo.
5. Use RANGE to set the output level, or patch CV into it to use it as a VCA.
sections.patching:
• Panning in a circle: Send the six outputs to the pan CVs of six mixer channels. With NODES at 0 the sounds sit evenly around the stereo field and rotate. A trigger into a PHASE RESET input groups them together in space, and then they slowly spread out again. Try other NODES settings to group them differently.

• Self-modulation: Patch one output into RATE and another into NODES, with a little attenuation on each. The six LFOs start bending each other's shapes.

• Audio-rate timbres: Turn on v/oct mode in the context menu. Patch output 2 into NODES with the attenuverter at 0.1 and listen to output 4. Turn NODES for timbre. Every output sounds different, so try them all.

name: Collatz
tagline: Rhythms from the Collatz conjecture. Pick a number and listen to it fall to 1.

sections.panelMap:
COLLATZ turns Collatz sequences into rhythm. Pick a starting number. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add one. Repeat. The Collatz conjecture says you always end up at 1, and when the module gets there it stops and sends an END gate.

Each number in the sequence becomes a burst of gates within one clock interval. MODULUS caps the bursts: the remainder (number mod MODULUS) sets how many pulses go to OUT, and the quotient sets the accents on ACC. The display shows the current number, the modulus, and the beats-to-accents split.

Controls (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- NUMBER: starting number, 2–1000.
- MODULUS: maximum pulses per clock interval, 1–100.

Jacks:
- CLOCK: required. The time between clock pulses sets the length of each burst.
- RESET: stops the sequence and turns the outputs off. Also has a button.
- START: arms a new run using the current NUMBER. It starts on the next clock pulse. Also has a button.
- OUT: the main gate bursts, 50% pulse width.
- ACC: accent gates.
- END: goes high when the sequence reaches 1. Patch END into START to loop.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a clock into CLOCK. Without a clock the module stays silent.
2. Set NUMBER and MODULUS. For drum patterns keep MODULUS low. Higher settings can run up to audio rate.
3. Press START or send it a trigger. The sequence begins on the next clock.
4. Patch OUT and ACC to drums.
5. Patch END into START to repeat the sequence forever.
sections.patching:
• Drums: The gates are short and snappy, which suits snares and percussion. Clock it from your main clock or a division, and patch END into START so it cycles.

• Simple patterns: Powers of two give plain, predictable runs, like rotating clock divisions:
  32→16→8→4→2→1
  8→4→2→1

• Nested patterns: Many sequences contain each other, so you can pick the length you want:
  12→6→3→10→5→16→8→4→2→1
  5→16→8→4→2→1

• Long walks: Small odd numbers can wander for a long time before landing. 9 takes 19 steps:
  9→28→14→7→22→11→34→17→52→26→13→40→20→10→5→16→8→4→2→1
  Every number always gives the same sequence, so you can come back to the ones you like. Some run for hundreds of steps, which is what RESET is for.

• Strumming: Use the bursts on OUT to pluck Karplus-Strong strings.

• Pattern variety: Keep NUMBER fixed and change MODULUS. The same sequence gives quite different drum patterns.

name: Strings
tagline: Six guitar strings as V/oct outputs. Pick chords from a button grid, with real fingerings, mutes, bends, capo and slash bass.

sections.panelMap:
STRINGS outputs six V/oct signals, one per string of a guitar, playing real chord fingerings. Choose chords from the button grid or by CV. The display shows the chord name and fingering. Bends, a whammy bar, a capo and a slash-bass input let you play it like a guitar.

Selecting chords:
- CHORD: chooses the column of the grid, 1–7.
- ROW: chooses the row, 1–4.
- Chord bank I and II: two gate inputs, each with a button. Together they pick one of four banks. Latching a button inverts its gate, so you choose which bank a high gate selects.
- BUTTONS: press any chord in the grid. The lit button shows the current chord's root, and the chord type is printed to the right of each row.

Changing the pitch:
- CAPO: transposes everything in semitones, -12 to +12. The CV input is V/oct: 1/12V per semitone, 1V per octave. Negative values tune the guitar down.
- PITCH BEND (one per string): bends that string up. The input is rectified, and 10V bends 2 semitones, so an envelope makes a natural bend.
- WHAMMY: the same bend applied to all six strings, on top of PITCH BEND.
- SLASH BASS: a V/oct note here becomes the bass note of the chord. STRINGS frets it on the low E or A string within reach of the chord shape and mutes any strings that would sound below it. If it can't be reached, the low string is retuned, like a drop tuning. Unpatched, chords play in root position.

Outputs:
- V/OCT OUT (6): one per string. Muted strings output -10V so you can use them as logic.
- MUTE (6): a gate is high when that string is muted in the current chord. Use it to silence the matching voice.
- TRIG: a trigger whenever the chord or fingering changes: a button press, or a change to CHORD, ROW, bank or CAPO.
- ROOT: the root note of the chord as V/oct, for a bass or another instrument.
Patch only the leftmost V/OCT or MUTE output and it becomes a 6-channel poly cable.

Context menu:
- Classical Chord Set: swaps the suspended chords for diminished ones (see banks below).
- CHORD input in V/oct: send a note into CHORD and STRINGS finds the nearest chord in the current row, adding a semitone of capo when it needs to.
- Invert Mute Gate Outputs: the MUTE outputs go high when a string plays, so they can open a VCA directly.
sections.basicUse:
1. Pick a chord:
   - Press a button, or set CHORD and ROW. The grid is laid out like this:
     Row 1: B E A D G C F
     Row 2: A D G C F Bb Eb
     Row 3: E A D G C Bb7 Abmaj
     Row 4: A D G C F Bb Eb

2. Pick a bank with the I and II gates or buttons:
   - (0,0) Bank 1: dominant 7th, major, minor, sus2. The everyday chords. Relative majors and minors sit next to each other, so moving between them is easy.
   - (1,0) Bank 2: barre chords (dominant 7th, major and minor barre) and 6ths, plus open B and E major in the top row. The minor row adds Bb7 and Abmaj.
   - (0,1) Bank 3: sus4, major 7th, minor 7th, 7sus4. Major and minor 7ths add tension. Row 3 adds an Ab7.
   - (1,1) Bank 4: add9, augmented, minor 6th, minor 9th. The colourful ones.
   With Classical Chord Set on: Bank 1 swaps sus2 for diminished, Bank 2 swaps 6th for diminished 7th, Bank 3 is 2nd, major 7th, minor 7th, 9th, and Bank 4 is 6th, 7+5, minor 6th, augmented.

3. Handle the mutes:
   - Many fingerings skip strings. Those strings output -10V, and their MUTE gate goes high. Use the gates to silence the matching voices.

4. Bend and slide:
   - Send envelopes to PITCH BEND for single-string bends, or to WHAMMY to bend them all.
   - Use CAPO to move up and down the neck. VCV OCT makes a nice front end for it.

5. Strum:
   - TRIG fires on every chord change. Use it to start a strum, for example through IMPULSE CONTROLLER.

6. Add a bass note:
   - Patch a V/oct note into SLASH BASS for chords like C/G or D/F#.
sections.patching:
• Guitar with TWANG: Patch the leftmost V/OCT output (a 6-channel poly cable) into TWANG's PITCH, and the leftmost MUTE output into TWANG's MUTE CV with its trim fully up. TWANG plays six strings, and every string STRINGS mutes in the fingering is palm-muted on the matching TWANG string. Patch TRIG into TWANG's PLUCK to strum the whole chord on every change.

• Bends: Patch TRIG into ENVELOPE ARRAY and send one envelope to the 5th string's PITCH BEND.

• Neck slide: Patch a decay envelope into CAPO. The capo moves in whole semitones, so it sounds like sliding down the frets.

• Glass slide: Patch a sine LFO at about 6 Hz, unipolar, into WHAMMY. Reset the LFO from TRIG so the vibrato starts with each chord.

• Play from a keyboard: Turn on CHORD input in V/oct, set the CHORD knob all the way down, and patch a keyboard or sequencer into CHORD. Use ROW and the bank gates to choose the chord type. For any root you send, STRINGS finds the nearest guitar fingering and adds capo if it needs to.

• Bass lines under chords: Hold a chord and sequence SLASH BASS to walk the bass note underneath it.

name: Ouros
tagline: A stereo phase-feedback oscillator, shown on a circular display. Like the ouroboros, it feeds on its own tail.

sections.panelMap:
OUROS is a stereo oscillator named after the ouroboros, the snake that eats its own tail. Two oscillators circle each other on a polar display. A second phase oscillator, fed back into the first, bends its waveform. NODE moves the phase relationship between unison, two groups, three groups and back. FEEDBACK sets how hard the snake bites.

Pitch:
- V/OCT knob and input: frequency, across 8 octaves. A polyphonic V/OCT turns on polyphony for the module and every CV input.
- FM: exponential FM, added to V/OCT, with an attenuverter.
- SYNC: hard-syncs the oscillator. The button resets it by hand.

Shape (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- FEEDBACK: amount of phase feedback. At zero you get a clean sine, and POS, NODE and MULTIPLY do nothing.
- MULTIPLY: frequency of the feedback oscillator, 1–10x. Like an FM operator ratio, it sounds best at whole numbers, so the knob is mapped to spend most of its travel near them.
- POS: where in the cycle the feedback lands, ±360°.
- NODE: number of repeating nodes in the feedback phase, 0–5.

Stereo (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- PHASE: turns both outputs around the phase circle together, ±360°.
- SPREAD: phase difference between left and right, ±360°.

Outputs:
- OUTS: left (orange on the display) and right (blue).

Context menu:
- Presets: factory presets in three groups. See below.

Technical notes

How does phase-feedback distortion work? The oscillator's phase isn't fixed. A portion of another oscillator's output is fed back to push its phase around. Like the ouroboros, it feeds on itself. Each cycle the phase is shifted a little off its ideal position, so the waveform bends and skews. The result is a sine-like signal whose harmonics and shape depend on the feedback depth: the more feedback, the more distortion.

[[fig:feedback]]

Why the MULTIPLY knob feels sticky: MULTIPLY scales the phase oscillator against the main one, much like an FM operator ratio, and it sounds best at whole-number ratios. The knob is mapped through a set of steep 5th-order curves, so it still covers the whole range but spends most of its travel close to whole numbers.

[[fig:multiply]]
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the pitch with V/OCT. Everything starts as a sine.

2. Add FEEDBACK. The waveform bends and picks up harmonics as you turn it up.

3. Shape it:
   - MULTIPLY picks the harmonic the feedback works on. Stay near whole numbers for in-tune, metallic tones.
   - NODE and POS change where and how often the feedback lands in each cycle.

4. Widen it:
   - SPREAD separates the left and right phases for stereo width and movement. PHASE turns both together.
   - The display draws the two outputs in polar form, so you can see what each change does.

5. Load a preset:
   - Right-click › Presets for classic waveforms, instruments and shapes. Use SYNC or its button to realign the phases after loading.
sections.patching:
• Classic waveforms: The default is a sine. The presets also give rounded saw, square and triangle. They're built additively, so they lack the very top harmonics, but they sound nice unfiltered.

• Instruments: Presets approximate piano, electric piano, violin, saxophone, flute, marimba and glass harp. Whole-number MULTIPLY values keep them harmonic.

• Shapes: The shape presets (Aardvark, Bunny, Butterfly, Rubber Ducky and more) all use whole-number MULTIPLY with SPREAD at zero. Nudge them slightly off for animated timbres and stereo movement.

[[fig:presets]]

• Stereo animation: Modulate SPREAD slowly and run the output through a chorus or delay.

• Metallic tones: Whole-number MULTIPLY with moderate FEEDBACK gives bright, bell-like partials.

• Controlled chaos: Patch an LFO into NODE or POS, and keep FEEDBACK below where it runs away.

The MULTIPLY knob's mapping. Each step is a steep curve, so most of the knob's travel sits close to a whole number.

name: Pressed Duck
tagline: A crunchy six-channel stereo mixer with sidechain ducking, compression and saturation.

sections.panelMap:
PRESSED DUCK compresses and ducks your sound into a deliciously crunchy mix. Six stereo channels are compressed together, and a stereo sidechain channel can duck all of them, which is great for pumping bass lines. Everything is under CV, and the saturation uses antiderivative anti-aliasing for a cleaner mix at low CPU.

Channels:
- SIDE: stereo sidechain input. It ducks the six main channels and sits in the centre of the mix. It isn't compressed.
- STEREO INPUTS: six stereo channels. A poly cable in channel 1 spreads across the six channels.
- LEVELS: sliders for input level, 0 to 2x. The middle mark is unity.
- VCA INPUTS: linear VCA CV, multiplied with the slider.
- PAN: one knob and CV per channel. SIDE doesn't pan.
- MUTES: clickless mute buttons with a smooth 5 ms fade. Shift-click a button to solo that channel.

Master (each with an attenuverter and CV):
- DUCK: how far the SIDE signal ducks the main mix.
- PRESS: compression of the main mix. The lights show how much is being applied.
- FEED: extra gain after the compressor, up to 11x, for pushing the saturation into distortion. The lights show how much clipping is happening.
- LEVEL: master level, up to 2x. At 1x the mix saturates at 5V; at 2x, at 10V.
- L / R: stereo outputs.

Context menu:
- Apply Filters: a 30 Hz high-pass on every input removes DC, which keeps the saturation cleaner. On by default.
- Muted Sidechain still Ducks: mute SIDE and it keeps ducking, so you can use a signal you don't want to hear (a kick, say) as the trigger.
- Enable Supersampling: oversamples the output saturation for less aliasing, at more CPU.
- Mute CVs function as Toggle: on by default, so each trigger into a mute input flips the mute. Turn it off and the CV holds the mute while it's high, overriding the button.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch up to six stereo sources, and a sidechain source into SIDE.
2. Set levels with the sliders. Use PAN to place each channel.
3. Turn up DUCK to make room for the sidechain. You can duck from the SIDE signal itself, or patch an envelope into the DUCK CV.
4. Add PRESS to glue the mix together. Fully compressed, the mix fills the whole range set by LEVEL, with tanh saturation.
5. Add FEED for drive and crunch. At extreme settings it will alias audibly; supersampling helps.
6. Set LEVEL for the output.
sections.patching:
• Plain mixer: Leave PRESS and FEED at zero.

• Sidechain pump: Kick into SIDE, bass and pads into the main channels. Set DUCK to taste. Turn on Muted Sidechain still Ducks and mute SIDE if you want the pump without hearing the kick.

• Chained ducking: Patch one PRESSED DUCK's output into the SIDE of the next. Duck the kick into the snare in the first, then the drum mix into the music in the second. Balance the DUCK levels carefully.

• Performance mutes: Bring channels in and out with the clickless mutes. The compressor keeps the overall level steady as channels come and go.

• Drive bus: Push FEED for tanh saturation across the whole mix.

name: Preeeeeeeeeeessed Duck
tagline: PRESSED DUCK, with sixteen channels. For when six just isn't enough.

sections.panelMap:
PREEEEEEEEEEESSED DUCK will satisfy your hunger and craving for more channels. It's PRESSED DUCK with sixteen stereo channels plus the sidechain: 34 audio inputs in 17 channels. Patch a fully loaded 16-voice polyphonic signal into the leftmost channel and duck into it with a SIDE signal.

Everything works the same as PRESSED DUCK:
- SIDE: stereo sidechain that ducks the main mix, with its own level slider and VCA input.
- STEREO INPUTS: 16 stereo channels, compressed together by PRESS. A poly cable in channel 1 spreads across all 16.
- VCA INPUTS / LEVELS: a slider (0 to 2x) and VCA input per channel.
- PAN: per channel.
- MUTES: clickless, with shift-click to solo.
- DUCK, PRESS, FEED and LEVEL, each with an attenuverter and CV.
- L / R outputs.

Context menu: Apply Filters, Muted Sidechain still Ducks, Enable Supersampling, and Mute CVs function as Toggle. See PRESSED DUCK for what each one does.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a polyphonic stereo source into channel 1, or up to 16 separate stereo sources.
2. Patch a kick or drum bus into SIDE.
3. Set DUCK for how much the mix gets out of the way, PRESS to glue it, FEED for crunch, and LEVEL for the output.
4. Use the clickless mutes to bring voices in and out.

See PRESSED DUCK for the details.
sections.patching:
• Big poly bus: Patch a 16-voice poly synth into channel 1 and pan each voice with the PAN knobs.

• Master bus: Use it as the main mixer for a whole rack, with the kick on SIDE.

• Staged ducking: Feed a PRESSED DUCK drum mix into SIDE, so the drums duck everything else.

name: Flower Patch
tagline: Turns audio into flowers. A 12-tone polar display with FFT, plus pitch and amplitude outputs for the strongest peaks.

sections.panelMap:
FLOWER PATCH draws your audio as a field of flowers. Each column of the display is one note of the 12-tone scale (C to B), and each row is an octave. The signal is drawn in polar form around each flower, with the period set by that flower's note, so each one shows how your audio lines up with that pitch. An FFT measures how much of each note is in the signal, and FLOWER PATCH also sends the strongest peaks out as V/oct.

Controls (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- HUE: colour of the display. Left gives monotone, desaturated colours; the middle gives white with the FFT peaks in colour; right gives a coloured background with the peaks highlighted.
- FILL: how much the shapes are filled in.
- FLOWER: morphs the shapes from rings into flowers.
- POWER: scales the shapes by the FFT result, positively or negatively, so loud notes grow (or shrink).

Jacks:
- IN: audio input. Left and right are averaged.
- OUT f: V/oct of the six strongest peaks, as a 6-channel poly cable.
- OUT A: the amplitude of each of those peaks, matching channel for channel.

Context menu:
- Flower Mode, Waterfall Mode, Scope Mode: three ways to draw the display.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch audio into IN.
2. Turn up FLOWER to grow petals, and FILL to fill them in.
3. Use POWER to make the notes in your signal stand out.
4. Pick colours with HUE.
5. Try the Waterfall and Scope views in the context menu.
sections.patching:
• Note watcher: Put FLOWER PATCH on a chord bus to see which notes are sounding.

• Pitch follower: Patch OUT f into a quantizer or oscillator to track the loudest pitches in a sound. Use OUT A as matching VCA levels to resynthesize the strongest partials.

• Light show: Patch slow LFOs into HUE, FILL and FLOWER and let the display move with the music.

name: Magnets
tagline: A magnetic spin lattice you can play with. 24 outputs read the average spin of each zone.

sections.panelMap:
MAGNETS, how do they work? This module runs a small magnetic spin-lattice simulation. Every light is one spin, flipping between up and down. Each spin is pulled toward the way its neighbours point and shaken up by temperature. The 24 outputs report the average spin in each zone of the grid, so you get 24 related, slowly shifting CVs.

Controls (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- TEMP: temperature. Cold and the lattice freezes into big stable regions. Hot and the spins flip constantly.
- POLARITY: pushes all the spins toward up or down, making them more likely to line up that way as they update.
- RATE: time between simulation updates, 0.15–2 ms. Faster updates use more CPU.
- INTERACT: how strongly each spin follows its neighbours. Low lets the lattice flow; high can trap it in a state.

Jacks:
- TAPE HEAD: sets the spins of the central square, and adds to POLARITY across the whole lattice. Write a signal into the middle and watch it spread.
- RESET: randomizes every spin, weighted by POLARITY. Also has a button.
- Outputs: 24 zones, one jack per zone of the grid.

Context menu:
- Voltage Range ±5V: switches the outputs from ±10V to ±5V.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set RATE. Start in the middle and only push it faster if you need to.
2. Set TEMP. Low freezes the lattice, high fills it with noise. Interesting things happen near the point where it starts to freeze.
3. Set INTERACT. Higher values make larger regions that move together, and can cause sudden phase changes.
4. Use POLARITY to lean the whole lattice one way.
5. Press RESET to scramble it and start again.
6. Patch any of the 24 outputs as CV. Neighbouring outputs move together.
sections.patching:
• Connected motion: Send neighbouring outputs to related parameters, like a filter's cutoff and resonance, or the pans of two voices. They move in a way that feels physically linked.

• Swells: Patch a slow LFO into POLARITY. The whole lattice tips toward positive, then negative, taking all 24 outputs with it.

• Slow drift: Low TEMP, moderate INTERACT and a slow RATE give slow, organic movement.

• New state every bar: Patch a clock division into RESET to snap the lattice into a fresh state on the downbeat.

• Writing into the lattice: Patch an LFO or a sequence into TAPE HEAD. It flips the centre spins, and the change ripples outward through the zones.

name: Syncro
tagline: Eight clocks from one, at any ratio. Rotate the ratios, add fills, and bend time with swing.

sections.panelMap:
SYNCRO is an eight-channel clock multiplier and divider. Each channel runs at its own fraction of the master clock. ROTATE moves the ratios between channels, FILL adds extra beats, and SWING bends the master clock itself, so every channel stays in step with it. FILL and ROTATE are made for self-patching new rhythms.

Master clock:
- Display: BPM to 0.1 BPM, and swing in %.
- CLOCK: master tempo, up to 480 BPM. The CV input adds 10 BPM per volt at full attenuverter (or tracks V/oct, see the context menu).
- EXT CLOCK: patch a clock here and SYNCRO follows it instead. The tempo comes from the time between the last two pulses.
- ON/OFF: starts and stops the clocks. A gate into the jack flips the button's state.
- RESET: restarts and resyncs every channel. Also has a button.

Shaping (each with an attenuverter and CV input):
- SWING: ±99%. Swing runs over two master clock beats and speeds the clock up and slows it down along a cosine. At 50% the clock swings between 1.5x and 0.5x speed. It's more like rubato than a classic shuffle; for a traditional feel, run the master clock at half tempo and use a x2 channel.
- ROTATE: rotates the ratios across the outputs. The triangle on the display marks where row 1 is.
- WIDTH: gate width, 50% by default. Each output compares a ramp against WIDTH, so with swing on, the gates come out uneven.

Channels (8 rows):
- X: multiply, 0–128. Set it to 0 to silence a row.
- 1/Y: divide, 1–256. The display shows each row's ratio.
- FILL: buttons and gate inputs, one per row. The FILL knob (0–8 beats, shown by the lights, with CV) sets how many beats are added to that row's multiplier at the start of a cycle.
- OUT and INV: a gate and an inverted gate for each row. The top pair is the master clock, which doesn't rotate.

Context menu:
- Phasor Mode: each row outputs a pair of 0–10V ramps instead of gates. WIDTH then sets the phase between the pair (50% by default).
- Clock CV as V/oct: the CLOCK input reads V/oct, with 0V = 120 BPM. The CLOCK knob and attenuverter are disabled, and the display shows a ▸ to tell you.

[[fig:swing]]
sections.basicUse:
1. Set the tempo with CLOCK, or patch a clock into EXT CLOCK.
2. Set a ratio for each row with X and 1/Y.
3. Patch the OUT and INV jacks to drums, sequencers and envelopes.
4. Add FILL to a row with its button or gate input for extra beats.
5. Turn ROTATE to move the ratios between outputs. The X and 1/Y knobs follow the rotation; the FILL inputs stay with their row.
6. Add SWING for a pushed-and-pulled feel.
sections.patching:
• Tap tempo: Patch VCV Push into EXT CLOCK. The button becomes a tap tempo.

• Fills: Set one of the bottom rows to a long division and patch its INV output into a drum row's FILL input. Patch another long division into the FILL CV so the fill size changes too.

• Synth pad: Turn on Clock CV as V/oct and patch a pitch into the CLOCK input. Set the rows to harmonic ratios like 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 6:1, 8:1. Mix the outputs in a mixer that can handle DC, like PRESSED DUCK, and shape the levels with ENVELOPE ARRAY.

• Muting rows by rotation: Set X to 0 on some rows. As ROTATE moves, different rows drop out.

• Swing and phasors: In Phasor Mode, patch the outputs into SIGNALS to watch swing bend the ramps.

[[fig:phasors]]

figures.caption: Swing at 50%. Over two clock beats the clock speeds up to 1.5x and slows to 0.5x along a cosine.
Phasor Mode outputs on SIGNALS.
With swing on, the ramps bend, so the same WIDTH gives uneven gates.

name: Nona
tagline: Nine channels of gain, offset and mixing for CV. Outputs normal down the module.

sections.panelMap:
NONA is a CV utility for scaling, offsetting and mixing signals. Use it to match voltage ranges between modules, make DC voltages, or mix CV.

Each of the nine rows has:
- IN: the signal to process.
- GAIN: -2x to +2x. Negative values invert, and gains over 1 boost weak signals.
- OFFSET: -10V to +10V. With nothing patched into IN, it's a plain DC voltage.
- OUT: the result. Each output also feeds the row below, so unpatched outputs mix down the module. Patching an OUT breaks the chain at that point.

Context menu:
- Row 1 as Master VCA: row 1 becomes a VCA for the other eight. Their outputs are multiplied by row 1's OUT, and a curved line appears on the panel to show it.

[[fig:master-vca]]
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch CV into any input.
2. Use GAIN to scale it (negative inverts) and OFFSET to shift it.
3. Take the output from that row, or leave it unpatched to mix it into the rows below.
4. With nothing patched in, use OFFSET as a DC voltage source.
sections.patching:
• Range matching: Turn a ±10V LFO into 0–5V with GAIN 0.25 and OFFSET 2.5V.

• Mixing: Patch several modulators into rows 1–8 and take the mix from OUT 9.

• Submixes: Patch OUT 3 and OUT 9 to get two separate mixes, rows 1–3 and rows 4–9.

• One knob for everything: Turn on Row 1 as Master VCA and patch an envelope into row 1. All eight other rows follow it.

figures.caption: With Row 1 as Master VCA on, a curved line marks row 1 as the VCA for the rows below.

name: Decima
tagline: A ten-step gate sequencer you program with buttons. Per-step probability, reversible, with a gate for every step.

sections.panelMap:
DECIMA is a ten-step gate sequencer. Click the buttons to set your pattern, click the step lights to jump anywhere, and give each step its own probability. Each step also has its own gate output, which makes it easy to self-patch shorter sequences.

Inputs:
- CLOCK: advances one step. The time between the last two clocks sets the length of the 50% gates.
- DIR: a positive voltage runs the sequence backwards.
- RESET: back to step 1.

Steps (10 rows):
- Button (left): turns the step on or off.
- STEP light: shows the active step. Click it to jump there.
- PROB: probability that an active step fires, 0–100%.
- GATE: 10V for the whole time this step is active, whether or not it fired.

Outputs:
- OUT: a 50% gate for each step that fires.
- INV: a 50% gate for each step that doesn't.

Context menu:
- Active step outputs to Gate output: the step GATE outputs follow OUT for their own step, instead of staying high for the whole step.
sections.basicUse:
1. Click the buttons to choose which steps play.
2. Patch a clock into CLOCK and take OUT to a drum or envelope.
3. Turn down PROB on any step to make it fire only some of the time.
4. Patch INV to a second voice for the off-beats.
5. For a shorter loop, patch a step's GATE output into RESET. Patching step 7 into RESET gives a six-step loop.
sections.patching:
• Hi-hats with life: Turn every step on and set PROB between 50% and 80%. The pattern stays busy but never repeats exactly.

• Call and response: OUT to one drum, INV to another. Every clock goes to exactly one of them.

• Odd lengths: Patch different step GATEs into RESET for 3, 5 or 7-step loops. Switch the RESET cable during a performance to change the meter.

• Ping-pong: Patch the GATE from step 10 into a flip-flop and drive DIR with it, so the sequence turns around at each end.

name: Morta
tagline: One knob, sixteen outputs. Every common range, forwards and backwards, plus a voltmeter.

sections.panelMap:
MORTA turns one knob into sixteen outputs, each scaled to a different range. Patch a CV into the input and MORTA turns the knob for you, and the display shows the voltage. It's useful for driving many parameters with one gesture, for measuring and rescaling signals, and with its reversed outputs, as a crossfade controller.

Top:
- Big knob: the master control, ±10V.
- Input jack: patch a CV to take over the knob. The knob then animates to follow it. The two small knobs beside it set input gain (±2x) and offset (±10V).
- Display: the current voltage.
- Pass-through output: the knob or input voltage, unchanged.
- POLYPHONY: a poly input switches the whole module to poly. The display shows the first channel.

RANGE knob, attenuverter and CV: sets R, the range of the fourth column, from 0 to 10V.

Outputs, in a 4 × 4 grid. Columns are 1V, 5V, 10V and R. Rows are:
- Unipolar: 0→1, 0→5, 0→10, 0→R
- Bipolar: -1→1, -5→5, -10→10, -R→R
- Reverse bipolar: 1→-1, 5→-5, 10→-10, R→-R
- Reverse unipolar: 1→0, 5→0, 10→0, R→0
sections.basicUse:
1. Turn the big knob, or patch a CV into the input.
2. Patch outputs from whichever rows and columns your destinations need.
3. Set RANGE for the fourth column, or modulate it.
4. Use the reversed rows where one thing should go down while another goes up.
sections.patching:
• Scene control: Map one MORTA across a mix: filters open, reverb rises, a sound fades out, all from one knob.

• Crossfader: Patch a unipolar output and its reversed partner into two VCAs. Turning the knob fades from one to the other.

• Rescaler: Patch a ±5V LFO into the input to get 0–10V, 0–1V or ±R copies of it at once.

• Voltmeter: Patch anything into the input to read its voltage on the display.

• Poly macro: Patch a poly modulation source into the input. Every output becomes a poly cable in its range.

name: Step Wave
tagline: An eight-step sequencer that draws a waveform. You shape each step, and move the boundaries between them.

sections.panelMap:
STEP WAVE is an eight-step sequencer that outputs a continuous waveform rather than plain steps. Each stage has a VALUE, a SHAPE and a number of BEATS, and you can push the boundaries between stages back and forth with CV. SLEW smooths over any jumps in the result.

The display shows the output in blue. With SLEW at 0, a grey line shows the waveform before slew. Along the bottom is the GATE output with its BEATS.

Timing:
- CLOCK: each clock sets the length of one stage (one grid line on the display). With no clock it runs at 120 BPM. The clock sets the timing only, it doesn't advance the stages, so use RESET to line up with your master clock.
- ON/OFF: starts and stops the sequencer. A gate into the jack pauses it while high. The button inverts what the gate does.
- RESET: back to the start of stage 1. Also has a button.

Stages (8 columns):
- VALUE slider: the stage's level, ±5V. A CV patched into the jack below takes over the slider, and the slider moves to show it.
- RHYTHMIC DISPLACEMENT knobs and jacks: between each pair of stages. They move the boundary earlier or later by up to half a stage (±5).
- SHAPE: morphs through 12 shapes for the stage's curve.
- BEATS: 1–10 gate subdivisions in the stage.
- STAGE buttons and outputs: click to jump to a stage (this also works while stopped). Each output carries a 10V gate for as long as its stage plays.

Global:
- LINK: with LINK on, the SHAPE repeats once per beat across the stage.
- TRACK: with TRACK on, each stage follows its VALUE CV continuously, even at audio rate. With it off, a stage samples its VALUE when it starts.
- SLEW: smooths the output. It's scaled to the stage length.
- CV OUT: the waveform.
- GATE OUT: gates for the BEATS, as drawn at the bottom of the display.

Context menu:
- Stage Value CV Modulates Shape: the VALUE inputs modulate each stage's SHAPE instead of its level.
- Quantize CV Out: rounds CV OUT to semitones.

[[fig:shapes]]
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a clock into CLOCK, and the same clock (divided) into RESET to keep the sequence lined up.
2. Set a VALUE for each stage.
3. Pick a SHAPE for each stage to decide how it moves from one value to the next.
4. Set BEATS for the rhythm on GATE OUT. Turn on LINK to repeat the shape on every beat.
5. Turn the RHYTHMIC DISPLACEMENT knobs to stretch some stages and squeeze others.
6. Add SLEW to smooth the result.
sections.patching:
• Melody with groove: CV OUT into a V/oct input with Quantize CV Out on, and GATE OUT into an envelope. Displacement swings the notes.

• Wobbly bass: Short CLOCK, LINK on, BEATS of 2 or 4 on some stages. CV OUT into a filter cutoff.

• Drifting groove: Patch slow LFOs into the RHYTHMIC DISPLACEMENT inputs so the boundaries breathe.

• Audio-rate waveform: Clock it fast with TRACK on and patch audio-rate signals into the VALUE inputs. STEP WAVE becomes a drawable oscillator.

• Animated shapes: Turn on Stage Value CV Modulates Shape and patch LFOs into the VALUE inputs to morph the shapes over time.

figures.caption: SHAPE morphs continuously through 12 shapes. The numbers show the knob positions in between.

name: Arrange
tagline: A seven-channel sequencer you can play into. Record CV, quantize it, or turn it into probability triggers.

sections.panelMap:
ARRANGE is a seven-channel step sequencer with up to 128 stages. Each channel can record its input, hold a knob setting, quantize to semitones, or fire probability triggers. Switch between record and playback as you go.

Transport:
- STAGE: selects the stage. Its range follows END.
- END: length of the sequence, up to 16 stages by default (up to 128 in the context menu). Changing it resets to stage 1.
- REC: arms recording, with a button and gate input. The light turns red.
- BACK / FWD: step backwards or forwards, with buttons and inputs.
- RESET: back to stage 1.

Display: the top shows the current stage and the sequence length, with a white dot for progress. The column below shows each channel's output as a voltage, a note, or a probability.

Channels (7 rows):
- IN: overrides the knob. A poly cable into IN spreads downward across the channels.
- MODE button: Voltage (off), V/oct semitones (blue), or Probability triggers (yellow).
- Knob: the stage value, ±10V.
- OUT: the current stage value. In Probability mode, -10V means 0% and +10V means 100%, and the output fires a trigger with that chance each time the stage is reached.

When REC is off, turning a knob changes the output but doesn't write to the sequence. When REC is on, the knob is ignored and the input is recorded into the active stage. Shift-click a knob while recording to apply its value to every stage.

Context menu:
- Set Max Sequence Length: up to 128, 256, 512, 1024 or 2048 stages, handy for quantizing long compositions to 16th notes.
- Stop Record At End: REC turns off when the sequence wraps, so you can record exactly one loop.
- Edit Mode: when on, moving to a stage while recording loads its stored values onto the knobs for editing. When off, the knobs stay where they are, which suits live recording.
- Set Polyphony for Channel 1: OUT 1 carries the channels as one poly cable.
- Copy Stage, Copy All Stages (up to current), Paste (insert after current), Clone Stage to All, Clear Stage, Add Stage (after current), Delete Stage: edit the sequence directly.
- Rotate Sequence to Start Here: the current stage becomes stage 1, and the stages before it wrap around to the end.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set END for the number of stages.
2. Clock FWD to play.
3. Set each channel's MODE: plain voltage, semitones, or probability.
4. To program by hand, step through with FWD and set the knobs with REC on.
5. To record, patch CV into IN, turn on REC and let it play through. Turn on Stop Record At End to capture one loop.
sections.patching:
• Automation lanes: Record slow knob gestures from MORTA or a MIDI controller and loop them.

• Live sampling: Punch REC in and out on a rhythm to catch snapshots of changing modulation.

• Probability drums: Set some channels to Probability mode and patch them to drums. Program a chance for each stage.

• Song structure: Set a long max length, clock FWD with a bar clock, and use the channels to change sections: transposition, mutes, effect sends.

name: Tri Delay
tagline: A stereo delay with three taps and a display that shows you what each tap is doing.

sections.panelMap:
TRI DELAY is a stereo delay with three taps. Each tap has its own time, feedback and pan, set as offsets from the master knobs. The display shows envelope followers for the dry input (orange) and wet output (blue), plus a dot for each tap: its position is the delay time, its size is the feedback, and its colour is the pan (red left, blue right). Gentle tanh saturation with anti-aliasing, and 8x oversampled outputs, keep the feedback from turning harsh.

Master controls (each with an attenuverter and CV):
- DELAY: master delay time, in ms.
- PAN: master pan. There are two delay lines, one per output, and each tap feeds both.
- FEEDBACK: master feedback, 0–100%.
- WET/DRY: mix, 50% by default.

Taps I, II and III: a trimpot for each of DELAY, PAN and FEEDBACK adds to or subtracts from the master. By default the taps are panned left, centre and right.

Buffer:
- BUFFER SIZE switch: 36 ms, 360 ms or 3600 ms. Delays up to 3.6 seconds. The same choice is in the context menu under Delay Time.
- CLEAR: empties the buffer, with a button and gate input.
- HOLD: loops what's in the buffer while the button or gate is held.

Jacks:
- IN L / R: a mono signal in L goes to both channels.
- OUT L / R.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch audio into IN and take OUT L and R.
2. Set DELAY and FEEDBACK with the master knobs.
3. Use the tap trimpots to spread the three taps apart in time, feedback and stereo position.
4. Set WET/DRY.
5. Press HOLD to loop the current buffer, and CLEAR to empty it.
sections.patching:
• Rhythmic echoes: Set the three taps to simple fractions of a beat, like 1/4, 3/8 and 1/2.

• Stereo shimmer: Short buffer, taps panned wide, and a slow LFO on DELAY.

• Freeze: Hold the buffer and modulate PAN and FEEDBACK for an evolving pad from a single phrase.

• Comb tones: The 36 ms buffer with high feedback turns the taps into pitched resonances.

name: Tatami
tagline: A stereo polyphonic wavefolder that weaves waveforms into new shapes instead of creasing them.

sections.panelMap:
TATAMI is a stereo, polyphonic wavefolder. SHAPE morphs smoothly between folding curves, and antiderivative anti-aliasing keeps the folds smooth, weaving waveforms into new shapes rather than creasing them. Separate DENSITY controls for left and right make stereo images out of a mono source.

Controls (each with an attenuator and CV input):
- SHAPE: the folding curve, 0–3. A saturating tanh at 0, a sine at 1, an exponential sine at 2, and back to tanh at 3.
- COMPRESS: squeezes the input before folding and expands it by the same amount afterwards, so dynamic signals fold evenly.
- SYMMETRY: adds a DC offset to the input before folding, ±5V. Shifts which harmonics come out.
- DENSITY L and R: how many times the signal folds, 1–20, set separately for each side, each with its own CV.

Jacks:
- IN L / R: stereo input, up to 16-channel polyphony.
- OUT L / R.

The display shows the folded output over the input.

Context menu:
- Apply DC Blocking Filter.
- Enable 8x Supersampling: less aliasing at high DENSITY, at more CPU.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch audio into IN and take OUT L and R.
2. Raise DENSITY for more folds. Set left and right a little apart for width.
3. Sweep SHAPE to choose the folding character.
4. Use SYMMETRY to bring in even harmonics.
5. Add COMPRESS if your input changes level a lot, such as a plucked or enveloped sound.
sections.patching:
• Moving timbre: A slow LFO on SHAPE gives a constantly changing tone.

• Stereo from mono: Patch a mono source into IN L and modulate DENSITY L and R from two different LFOs.

• Folded FM: Fold a sine before using it as an FM modulator, for brighter, more controllable sidebands.

• Envelope-driven folds: Send an envelope to DENSITY so each note starts bright and settles.

name: Cartesia
tagline: A 4×4×4 sequencer you can move through in three dimensions, with knob ranges under CV.

sections.panelMap:
CARTESIA is a 4×4×4 sequencer: four layers (Z) of 4×4 grids (X and Y). The display shows exactly where you are in the cube, and the 16 knobs and buttons always edit the layer you're looking at. CV over the knobs' range adds a twist: the same pattern can be stretched, squashed or shifted live.

Display and slice panel:
- 3D display: the cube, with the current step lit. The four buttons above select which Z layer the knobs show.
- 16 knobs: the step values for the shown layer. The colour shows the layer. Each knob's display shows its note or voltage.
- Buttons by each knob: turn that step's gate on or off.

Moving through the cube (each row has a CV input, a reverse trigger and a forward trigger with button):
- X, Y, Z: step along each axis, or set the position directly with CV.
- SCAN: walks through the current layer in X–Y order.

Ranges:
- MIN and RANGE: the lowest knob value, ±10V, and the span of the knobs, 1–20V. Both have an attenuverter and CV, and the knob displays update as they move.
- QUANTIZE: switches between semitone notes and plain voltages.
- OFFSET: CV added to the final output.

Buttons and inputs:
- ON/OFF: stops and starts the sequencer.
- RESET: back to the first step.
- RANDOM: jumps to a random X, Y, Z position.

Outputs:
- RESET: a trigger whenever the sequencer resets.
- TRIG.: a trigger on every step.
- POLY: 1–4. Sets how many layers come out at once. OUTPUT, GATE and INV become poly cables carrying the selected layer and the ones after it.
- GATE / INV.: the gate and inverted gate for the current step's button.
- OUTPUT: the sequencer value.

Context menu:
- Copy Layer, Paste Layer, Paste to All Layers.
- Sample and Hold Active Step: on by default. OUTPUT only updates on steps whose gate is on, and holds through the steps that are off.
- Enable Triggers from Gate Outputs: GATE and INV send short triggers instead of full-length gates.
sections.basicUse:
1. Pick a layer with the buttons above the knobs, and set the 16 values.
2. Turn on the steps you want with the buttons.
3. Clock X FWD to walk across the layer. Clock Y and Z from slower divisions to move to the next row and layer.
4. Or clock SCAN FWD to step through a layer in order.
5. Set MIN and RANGE, and turn on QUANTIZE for melodies.
6. Turn up POLY to play several layers in parallel.
sections.patching:
• Song sections: Write a different phrase on each layer. Clock X and Y for the melody and advance Z each section.

• Four-voice harmony: Set POLY to 4 and send OUTPUT to a poly oscillator. Each layer is one voice.

• Stretchable patterns: Modulate RANGE slowly. The melody keeps its shape but its intervals grow and shrink.

• Controlled wandering: Trigger RANDOM occasionally between regular clocks to jump to somewhere new in the cube.

name: Junk DNA
tagline: A gate sequencer that writes and reads DNA. Type a pattern, and it grows into a 2056-letter gene with variations.

sections.panelMap:
JUNK DNA is a gate sequencer that generates and reads DNA. Type a repeat pattern in letter code, and it's copied out to fill a 2056-letter gene. Letters can be fixed bases or wildcards that are filled in at random on every repeat, so you can write anything from short repetitive motifs to whole genes. Each position then fires the gates for the base it holds.

[[fig:codes]]

REPEAT PATTERN: the text box. Use the IUPAC nucleotide codes:
- A, T, C, G: the four bases.
- R (A or G), Y (C or T), S (C or G), W (A or T), K (G or T), M (A or C): a random choice of two.
- B (not A), D (not C), H (not G), V (not T): a random choice of three.
- N: any base.
- X: a strand break. No base, so every gate is off at that position. Use it for rests.
An R has a 50% chance of being A or G. A D has a 33% chance each of being A, G or T.

Moving:
- FWD and REV: step forwards or backwards through the gene, with buttons. It wraps around at the ends.
- RESET: back to position 0. As long as the pattern doesn't change, the gene replays exactly.

Outputs, laid out on the Venn diagram:
- A, T, C, G: high while the current base is that letter.
- R, Y, S, W: high while the current base is either of their two letters.
- B, D, H, V: high while the current base is not their letter.
- N (centre): a trigger at every position.
- DNA: a voltage for the current base. A = 0V, T = 1V, C = 2V, G = 3V by default.
- P (bottom right): all twelve gates in one poly cable, in the order A, T, C, G, R, Y, S, W, D, H, V, B.

Gates stay high through repeats, so AAA gives one long gate on A. The same goes for the pattern outputs: CGCGCG keeps S high the whole time.

Context menu:
- Output Pulses instead of Gates: every position sends a short trigger instead of holding the gate.
- The DNA output voltage for each base can be set to your own values.
sections.basicUse:
1. Type a pattern into REPEAT PATTERN, for example CGNNNRX or ATTAGCC.
2. Clock FWD.
3. Patch A, T, C and G to four drum sounds, or use the R, Y, S, W and B, D, H, V outputs for broader patterns.
4. Patch RESET to replay the same gene from the start.
sections.patching:
• Four-piece kit: A to kick, T to snare, C to closed hat, G to open hat. Use fixed letters for the backbone and wildcards to vary the fills.

• Long and short gates: Patterns with runs (AAAA) make long gates; alternating patterns (ATATAT) keep W high. Use the pattern outputs for accents and structure.

• Melodies: Send DNA into a quantizer and set the base voltages to the notes you want.

• Poly gates: Patch P into a poly envelope or poly drum module to get all twelve gates in one cable.

figures.caption: The IUPAC nucleotide codes JUNK DNA understands, as listed in its context menu.

name: Picus
tagline: A two-voice drum pattern generator. Seven stages of clock ratios with a ten-step DON/KA pattern on top.

sections.panelMap:
PICUS is a two-channel trigger burst generator. Program up to seven stages, each with its own clock ratio. A variable-length beat pattern sits over the beats and decides which go to DON (the big drum) and which go to KA (the rim), so a simple interface gives complex rhythms.

Pattern (top row):
- Ten pattern buttons. Each press cycles DON (large white), KA (medium blue) and off (small red). Each beat in a stage plays the next step of the pattern.
- PATTERN LEN.: pattern length, 1–10 steps, with attenuverter and CV.

Stages (seven rows):
- SELECT: jumps to that stage when the current one ends.
- BEATS (− / +): beats to play in the stage. 0 mutes the stage.
- CYCLES (− / +): length of the stage in clock cycles. 0 turns the stage off, so it's skipped.
- The display shows each stage as BEATS:CYCLES. 2:1 plays two beats in one clock cycle; 3:4 plays three beats spread over four cycles.

Transport:
- Mode switch: O (off), I (on), or 1 (one-shot, which switches itself off at the end of the cycle).
- CLOCK: the master clock. It also accepts the CHAIN signal from HAMMER.
- RESET: back to the first stage and the start of the pattern. Also has a button.

Outputs:
- DON and KA: trigger outputs, as programmed by the pattern.
- END: a pulse at the end of each stage, or at the end of the loop (see the context menu).

Context menu:
- END outputs pulse at: each stage end, or the loop end.
- Pattern resets: at each stage end, or only on RESET.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a clock into CLOCK, or the CHAIN output of a HAMMER.
2. Set BEATS and CYCLES for each stage you want. Set CYCLES to 0 to skip a stage.
3. Click the pattern buttons to choose DON, KA or off for each step, and set PATTERN LEN.
4. Switch to I to play.
5. Patch DON and KA to two drum sounds.
sections.patching:
• Taiko: DON to a low drum, KA to a rim click. Mix stages like 1:1, 2:1 and 3:2 for rolling rhythms.

• Fills: Make the last stage fast (4:1 or 6:1) for a fill at the end of each loop.

• One-shot phrases: Set the switch to 1 and trigger RESET to play the sequence once.

• Linked to HAMMER: Patch HAMMER's CHAIN into PICUS for sample-accurate timing with your other clocks.

name: Node
tagline: A small two-channel stereo mixer and crossfader with clickless mutes and up to 10x gain.

sections.panelMap:
NODE is a compact two-channel stereo mixer and crossfader. Each channel has a VCA with up to 10x gain to lift weak signals, gentle tanh saturation at high gain, and clickless mutes.

Channels I and II (each):
- Inputs L and R. Mono and poly inputs are mixed down to one stereo channel.
- GAIN: 0–10x. At high gain the signal saturates gently, with antiderivative anti-aliasing.
- CV: a VCA input for the gain.
- MUTE: clickless mute. Bright red means muted.

Centre:
- XFADE: blends between channel I and channel II. The CV input takes -5V to +5V and moves the slider so you can see the mix.
- VOL.: output volume.
- OUT L / R.

Context menu:
- Output poly instead of mix: keeps poly inputs as poly cables at the output.
- Sum poly channels (instead of average).
- Mute Fade Time: 1 ms to 4 seconds, 10 ms by default.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch two stereo sources into channels I and II.
2. Set GAIN for each. Push it high for warmth.
3. Use XFADE to blend between them, by hand or with CV.
4. Use the MUTE buttons to bring them in and out. Lengthen the fade time in the context menu for slow swells.
sections.patching:
• Crossfade between scenes: Patch two textures in and move XFADE slowly with an LFO.

• CV booster: Turn GAIN up to lift a small modulation signal to full range.

• Dry and driven: Send the same signal into both channels, one with low GAIN and one with high, and use XFADE as a drive control.

• Long fades: Set the mute fade time to a few seconds and use the MUTE buttons as fade-ins and fade-outs.

name: Weave
tagline: A six-voice chord quantizer with guitar-like voicings. Weave the voices into new orders as you play.

sections.panelMap:
WEAVE is a chord quantizer with voicings that feel like guitar chords. It's built for strumming the six output voices like strings, or spreading them out in space. Each trigger weaves the six voices into a new order, so the same chord keeps moving.

Chord:
- NOTE: root note, as V/oct. The keyboard display shows it, and its − and + buttons move it down or up an octave.
- CHORD: chord type: Oct, M, m, 7, M7, m7, 6, m6, 9, M9, m9, Add9, sus2, sus4, 5, aug, dim. The CV input advances one type per semitone and wraps around (CV skips Oct). The display shows the chord name.
- SHIFT: adds directly to every output to transpose the voicing. Has a CV input.

Weaving:
- WEAVE: picks one of 21 orderings for how the voices move. Has an attenuverter and CV, 1V per pattern.
- TRIG.: moves to the next arrangement. Also has a button.
- RESET: back to the default order. Also has a button.
- Display: the notes on the six outputs. Each line shows the next arrangement that will come with a trigger.

Outputs:
- 1–6: the six voices.
- ROOT: the root note.
- TRIG: a trigger whenever a note changes.
- POLY: all six voices as one poly cable.

Context menu:
- Quantize Shift to semitones.
- Allow input to track multiple octaves: NOTE follows the octave of its input, instead of folding to one octave.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a root note into NOTE, or play the keyboard.
2. Choose a chord type with CHORD.
3. Patch outputs 1–6 to six voices, or POLY to one poly voice.
4. Send triggers to TRIG. to weave the voices into new orders. Choose how they move with WEAVE.
5. Use SHIFT to transpose the voicing.
sections.patching:
• Strummed guitar: Send outputs 1–6 to six plucked voices and trigger them one after another, for example from IMPULSE CONTROLLER.

• Moving in space: Pan each output to a different place. Each trigger moves the notes between positions.

• Chord progressions: Sequence NOTE and CHORD from a sequencer, and use TRIG on every beat to keep the voicing alive.

• Chords for MIRAGE: Patch POLY into MIRAGE's chord input to give it a live chord to quantize a melody against.

name: Wonk
tagline: Six LFOs locked to your clock, with phase-feedback distortion that goes from in sync to wonky without losing the beat.

sections.panelMap:
WONK is a six-channel LFO with built-in phase-feedback distortion. It morphs six synchronized oscillators into more chaotic shapes that still stay locked to the clock.

Top:
- CLOCK: syncs the LFOs to an external clock. Without one they run at 30 BPM.
- RESET: resets the oscillators. Also has a button.
- RATE X: multiplies the clock with positive values or divides it with negative values, from -24 to +24. Anything between -1 and 1 runs at 1x. Has an attenuverter and CV.

Shaping (each with an attenuverter and CV):
- WONK: amount of phase feedback. As it rises, the range of NODES narrows and the outputs morph from unison into chaos.
- FDBK POS.: which of the six channels the feedback comes from.
- NODES: phase spacing between the oscillators, -3 to +3.
- MOD DEPTH: output level, 0–5V.

Outputs:
- 1–6: the six LFOs. The display shows each one's current value.
- P: all six as one poly cable.

Context menu:
- Unipolar mode (0-10V): unipolar outputs instead of ±5V.
sections.basicUse:
1. Patch a clock into CLOCK.
2. Set RATE X: 2 for twice the clock, -4 for a quarter.
3. Set NODES to spread the six LFOs out in phase.
4. Raise WONK to bend them away from clean sines. They wander, but stay on the beat.
5. Patch RESET at the start of each bar if you want them to realign.
sections.patching:
• Tempo-locked mod bus: Clock it from your master clock and send the six outputs to filters, pans and VCAs. Everything moves in time.

• Controlled wobble: Push WONK for drift. Reset every bar so it never wanders too far.

• Poly LFO: Patch P into a poly VCA or filter so each voice gets its own related LFO.

• Breathing chaos: Send a slow LFO to WONK so the six channels drift from unison into chaos and back.

videos.title: New Modules, September 2025

name: Hammer
tagline: A sample-accurate eight-channel clock. Set ratios with buttons, add swing, and chain it to other HAMMERs and PICUS.

sections.panelMap:
HAMMER is a sample-accurate clock with eight channels. Each channel multiplies and divides the master clock to make any beat ratio or polyrhythm. Its CHAIN output carries the clock, on/off and reset to other HAMMER and PICUS modules.

Master clock:
- Display: tempo in BPM.
- RATE: master tempo, up to 480 BPM, with an attenuverter and CV. The CV adds 10 BPM per volt, or tracks V/oct (see the context menu).
- CLOCK input: follow an external clock instead. It also accepts the CHAIN signal from another HAMMER.
- CLK output: the main clock.
- SWING: ±99%. Clock multiples swing along with the master.
- ON/OFF: starts and stops the clock outputs, with a button and gate input.
- RESET: resets the clock dividers, with a button and gate input.

Channels:
- RATIO: each row has − and + buttons on both sides of the display. The left pair sets the multiplier, the right pair the divider. The display shows each ratio; "off" means the channel is silent.
- ROTATE: rotates the ratios across the outputs, with an attenuverter and CV. The ▸ marks where channel 1 is.
- Outputs 1–8: 50% gates at each channel's ratio.

Chaining:
- CHAIN: the internal, unswung master clock plus the ON/OFF and RESET state. Patch it into the CLOCK input of another HAMMER or PICUS. You can have one copy with swing and one without, or one in Phasor Mode.
- POLY: all eight gates in channels 1–8, and their inverted gates in channels 9–16.

Context menu:
- Phasor Mode: outputs 0–10V ramps instead of gates.
- Clock CV as V/oct, or Clock CV is 1V/10BPM.
- Channel Multiply/Divide: sliders for each channel, for typing exact values.
sections.basicUse:
1. Set RATE, or patch a clock into CLOCK.
2. Set each channel's ratio with the − and + buttons. 2:1 is twice the tempo, 1:3 is a third.
3. Patch the outputs to drums and envelopes.
4. Add SWING to taste.
5. Use ROTATE to move the ratios around the outputs.
sections.patching:
• Polyrhythm grid: Set a different ratio on each channel and patch them to percussion for interlocking rhythms.

• Swing and straight: Chain a second HAMMER from the first. Swing one and leave the other straight, both perfectly in time.

• Ramps: Turn on Phasor Mode and use the outputs as eight tempo-locked ramps for filters, panning or wavefolding.

• Drum patterns: Chain into PICUS so its DON and KA patterns follow HAMMER's clock.
